slides.title:
YOUR BOTS
WORK FOR YOU
slides.body: Assistants that organize daily work and act for people and businesses.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: Turn separate assistants into a working team.
bullets: Everyday access through the BotBar keyboard.
Business services through BotBoozle.

expanded.title: A request can become a completed next step
body: People spend time sorting messages, chasing replies and carrying context between apps. BotBar aims to let their assistants organize the work, reach the right service and return a useful result.
The business combines a familiar consumer access point with an enterprise offer, a directory of accepted relationships and a marketplace for useful bots.

slides.sourceLabel: Product vision and investment opportunity / November 2026

slides.title:
INBOXES
INTERRUPTIONS
UNFINISHED WORK
slides.body: Each message can create another task to organize, schedule or chase.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: The customer pays for the gaps between systems.
bullets: Important requests compete with unwanted alerts.
People reconcile calendars and repeat the same context.

expanded.title: The burden is deciding what deserves action
body: An inbox is only the start. A person still has to identify the request, collect a document, compare availability and follow through. Businesses carry the same burden when customers move between departments or suppliers.
Microsoft reported 117 emails a day and 153 Teams messages per weekday in its Microsoft 365 telemetry. BotBar targets the organizing and follow-through work around that communication.

rows.label: Workload evidence
rows.detail: Microsoft WorkLab, June 17, 2025. Microsoft 365 population, excluding EU and education tenants. These figures do not describe every consumer.

rows.label: Intended value
rows.detail: Fewer unnecessary interruptions and a clear next step when attention is needed.

slides.sourceLabel: Microsoft: 117 emails/day and 153 Teams messages/weekday. M365 telemetry, excluding EU and education tenants.

slides.title:
ASSISTANTS
ACTING FOR YOU
slides.body: Your bot prepares the request. An accepted company handle reaches the right business bot.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: Keep the work connected across channels.
bullets: Relevant context accompanies the task.
The answer, document or booking returns to you.
You approve the next step at your chosen level.

expanded.title: A reusable relationship across company boundaries
body: A customer asks their assistant to arrange a service. Their team organizes the request and the information they allow it to share. An accepted business handle provides a repeatable way to reach the appropriate company bot.

The business returns availability, a quote or a document. The customer sees the outcome and can approve the next action. Supported workflows should preserve the useful context instead of making either side start again.

rows.label: For people
rows.detail: An organizer that can prepare work and complete supported actions.

rows.label: For businesses
rows.detail: A consistent way to receive a permitted request and return a useful result.

slides.sourceLabel: Intended supported workflow. Actions depend on connected services, permissions and launch availability.

slides.title:
HOW THE
BUSINESS EARNS
slides.body: Customers pay for useful work. Partners pay for relevant, chosen discovery.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: Each revenue stream has a customer and a reason to pay.
bullets: Subscriptions and enterprise licenses.
Paid communication or compute usage.
Commission on creator marketplace sales.
Opt-in sponsored keys and store placements.

expanded.title: Each revenue stream has a buyer and a reason to pay
body: Individuals and teams can subscribe for recurring organization and collaboration. Organizations can license BotBoozle, including white-label services, deployment and support. Usage fees can cover selected services with variable costs.
Creators sell useful bots and the platform earns an agreed marketplace commission. Partners can purchase clearly identified keys or store placements when users choose sponsored discovery.

rows.label: Recurring revenue
rows.detail: Paid accounts and contracted enterprise fees.

rows.label: Usage revenue
rows.detail: Billable units multiplied by the agreed unit price.

rows.label: Marketplace revenue
rows.detail: Eligible completed transaction value multiplied by the agreed commission. Creator sales volume is not platform revenue.

rows.label: Discovery revenue
rows.detail: Eligible sponsored placements or advertising inventory, subject to user choice and commercial terms.

slides.sourceLabel: Proposed commercial model. Prices, commissions and contracts remain launch decisions.

slides.title:
BOTBAR
WHERE YOU TYPE
slides.body: The keyboard puts a person's bot team beside the work already on their screen.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: Own an everyday point of access.
bullets: Type, speak or reach a familiar bot.
Use permitted context in supported app work.
Return to useful services through visible keys.

expanded.title: Daily access can turn a useful action into a habit
body: BotBar is the everyday entry point. Its keyboard brings assistants close to the places where people write, communicate and act, reducing the effort of switching to a separate workflow.
That access also supports distribution. A person can keep useful bots close at hand, discover services and revisit a creator or business. Sponsored keys remain optional, identified placements.

rows.label: Consumer offer
rows.detail: Accessible keyboard and bot-team entry, with optional paid services.

rows.label: Distribution value
rows.detail: Repeat access at the moment a person needs help, rather than relying only on a store visit.

slides.sourceLabel: Illustrated product vision. Supported screen actions require OS capabilities and user permissions.

slides.title:
A REQUEST
BECOMES A RESULT
slides.body: “Find a service time that works for me and bring back the options.”
slides.alt: Concept illustration: Each participant contributes to the same outcome.
bullets: Prepare the request and permitted availability.
Ask the accepted business contact.
Return the options for confirmation.

expanded.title: The useful outcome is a decision someone can make
body: The personal assistant prepares the request, gathers permitted context and contacts the business through an accepted handle. The business bot can return available times or ask for missing information.
The customer receives a clear choice. Once they approve, a supported booking can complete and return its confirmation. The same pattern applies to a quote, a service update or a requested document.

rows.label: Customer control
rows.detail: The owner chooses which information and actions the assistants may use.

rows.label: Business value
rows.detail: A clearer request, less repetition and an observable next step.

slides.sourceLabel: Illustrative customer workflow, not a claim of a universally available booking integration.

slides.title:
BOTBOOZLE
FOR BUSINESS
slides.body: An organizational offer for companies that want to deploy and support their own bot services.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: Sell a recurring business job with a clear owner.
bullets: Enterprise licenses and supported deployments.
Branded services for partners and agencies.
Customer workflows connected through accepted handles.

expanded.title: The enterprise buyer pays for an operating service
body: BotBoozle is the enterprise and white-label offering. A company can provide its own customer-facing bot services while using the network to receive approved requests and coordinate with customers or other businesses.
The commercial offer can include platform access, deployment, management and support. A focused first contract establishes a useful job and its service requirements before expanding to more teams.

rows.label: Buyer
rows.detail: Service-business owners, customer-operations teams, agencies and distribution partners.

rows.label: Reason to pay
rows.detail: A supported workflow and a branded customer experience, with clear responsibilities and service terms.

slides.sourceLabel: Enterprise product direction. Availability, deployment scope and pricing depend on customer agreements.

slides.title:
YOUR HANDLE
YOUR RELATIONSHIPS
slides.body: People control their handles. BotBar operates the directory and marketplace around them.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: An address people can build a relationship around.
bullets: Choose the bots and contacts that belong to you.
Accept relationships before sharing work.
Return to a known person or company team.

expanded.title: A memorable address becomes an ongoing relationship
body: A handle should let someone reach the right bot team again without rediscovering the device, provider or conversation. The owner controls the handle, its bots and the relationships through which information can flow.

The platform operates registration, admission standards, discovery and store services. Its revenue comes from agreed products and transactions. Commercial terms define the services, transactions and sharing that each owner chooses.

rows.label: Owner control
rows.detail: Identity, contacts, permissions and the information shared for each job.

rows.label: Operator role
rows.detail: Directory and marketplace operations, admission standards and agreed commercial services.

slides.sourceLabel: Identity and permission design. Authentication and vetting support safer handoffs; they do not guarantee safety.

slides.title:
THE WORK
ON ONE BOARD
slides.body: A workspace for the assistants, conversations and results behind the task.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: Make collaboration understandable and usable.
bullets: See which participants contribute.
Keep the work and its returned result together.
Continue a project without rebuilding its context.

expanded.title: People can see the team while the task progresses
body: BotBoard gives the shared work a visible home. The intended experience lets someone understand which assistants are involved, what each contributed and what still needs a decision.
A team may agree on most of a question while one participant has a useful reservation. That brief difference should remain available. The person can consider it, move on or stop the work.

rows.label: User value
rows.detail: A clear view of the task and result, with attention reserved for meaningful choices.

rows.label: Commercial role
rows.detail: A home for ongoing collaboration and optional paid team services.

slides.sourceLabel: Illustrated design vision. The artwork is not a runtime acceptance screenshot.

slides.title:
ONE TEAM
SEVERAL CHANNELS
slides.body: Use voice when discussion helps and messages or files when the work needs them.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: Let the channel serve the job.
bullets: People and assistants can contribute to a task.
Background exchanges can support the discussion.
Meeting and phone options extend future workflows.

expanded.title: The channel should suit the job
body: A customer may want to speak while the assistants exchange information and prepare a result. A document, message or email can carry detail that does not need another spoken turn.

Zoom and Microsoft Teams are integration goals. Telephone, SMS and other communication services can add paid options where supported. These goals do not imply a partnership or a tested, generally available meeting integration.

rows.label: Experience goal
rows.detail: Relevant discussion alongside useful work, with the person able to interrupt or stop.

rows.label: Paid options
rows.detail: Supported external communication services with transparent usage terms.

slides.sourceLabel: Communication and meeting roadmap. Provider availability and permissions apply.

slides.title:
FEWER PINGS
CLEARER NEXT STEPS
slides.body: The goal is useful communication from accepted relationships, with less unwanted noise.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: The customer pays for the gaps between systems.
bullets: Let assistants organize progress before alerting you.
Control which contacts and services can reach you.
Use authenticated, permitted handoffs.

expanded.title: Attention and permissions remain with the owner
body: Routine updates can become a concise result instead of another stream of notifications. Accepted contacts and clear sharing choices are intended to reduce unwanted outreach and make requests easier to evaluate.

Authentication, bot admission and careful handling of shared material support safer interactions. They do not eliminate spam, malware or fraud. Users still need understandable controls, error recovery and a way to stop.

rows.label: Intended benefit
rows.detail: Less unnecessary interruption and fewer repeated requests for the same context.

rows.label: Control
rows.detail: Accept, limit or end relationships and choose when a task needs personal attention.

slides.sourceLabel: Intended benefits, not absolute guarantees of safety or freedom from unwanted messages.

slides.title:
CREATORS
BRING USEFUL BOTS
slides.body: A creator can build a service, reach customers and earn from repeated use.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: Connect the point of discovery to repeat use.
bullets: Customers discover bots for a specific job.
Useful bots join the customer's own team.
The platform earns an agreed sales commission.

expanded.title: Discovery can become a lasting customer relationship
body: The marketplace connects a creator's service with a person or company that needs it. The useful outcome matters more than a long catalogue: find the right bot, understand its offer and return to it through a familiar handle or key.

Creators retain their agreed proceeds and responsibilities. BotBar operates its store and earns the contracted platform share on eligible transactions. Marketplace sales volume and platform revenue remain separate measures.

rows.label: Creator value
rows.detail: Distribution, a recognizable identity and access to customers.

rows.label: Customer value
rows.detail: A way to find, compare and revisit useful services.

rows.label: Revenue basis
rows.detail: Completed eligible sales multiplied by the actual commission, after applicable commercial adjustments.

slides.sourceLabel: Marketplace business model. Seller terms, payment operations and commission require launch readiness.

slides.title:
DISCOVERY
BY USER CHOICE
slides.body: Relevant partners can pay for visible discovery when people choose to receive it.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: An address people can build a relationship around.
bullets: Clearly identified sponsored keyboard keys.
Promoted store listings and eligible referrals.
User choice governs the sponsored experience.

expanded.title: A useful placement earns attention
body: A visible key can help a person find a relevant business or bot at the moment they need it. Store promotion offers another route to discovery. Partners pay for eligible placement or agreed advertising inventory.
The intended model is opt-in and clearly labeled. Users choose sponsored discovery and control what information is shared. Reach, engagement and customer results determine placement value.

rows.label: Partner buyer
rows.detail: Businesses and creators seeking relevant, measurable exposure.

rows.label: User control
rows.detail: Whether to receive sponsored discovery, which services to keep and what information to share.

slides.sourceLabel: Proposed opt-in advertising and partner model. Placement and revenue terms remain commercial decisions.

slides.title:
EXISTING BUDGETS
FOR CUSTOMER WORK
slides.body: Illustrative annual company revenue at 0.25% of each reported market.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: Start with budgets already committed to customer work.

expanded.title: A focused workflow can earn a share of established spending
body: Cloud contact centers and sales software are existing spending categories. BotBar’s entry is a focused coordination workflow, sold to buyers responsible for follow-up, service and team productivity.

Using the published annual revenue bases, a 0.25% share corresponds to $21 million in contact centers or $64.25 million in CRM sales software. The opportunity is to earn a small share of established spending through useful customer workflows.

rows.label: How revenue is earned
rows.detail: Team services, subscriptions and supported workflow or communication usage.

rows.label: What the calculation means
rows.detail: Market size × 0.0025. Conditional annual revenue, not profit, achieved share or a forecast. These overlapping markets are not added together.

slides.sourceLabel: USD. Reported market estimates × 0.25%; conditional revenue, not a forecast. Markets are not additive.

slides.title:
COMMUNICATION
AND DISCOVERY
slides.body: Two additional revenue mechanisms, with different buyers and market boundaries.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: Two additional ways to earn from useful adoption.

expanded.title: Broader spending is a reference point, not a forecast
body: Communication services address businesses paying to connect conversations and workflows. Advertising and sponsorship address suppliers paying for relevant discovery. These are different buyers and different revenue mechanisms.

At 0.25% of the reported annual market revenue, programmable communications represents $37.25 million; U.S. display advertising represents $204 million. The advertising category is a broad opportunity reference, not a measured bot-keyboard market.

rows.label: Communication services
rows.detail: Paid messaging, voice and white-label offers for businesses using the network.

rows.label: Discovery
rows.detail: Opt-in sponsored keyboard keys and identified store placements. Advertising reach and demand still have to be established.

rows.label: Market boundaries
rows.detail: Independent opportunities with different scopes. Do not add these figures to the previous page or treat them as a minimum return.

slides.sourceLabel: USD. 0.25% share calculation, not a forecast. Broad adjacent markets; not BotBar’s measured serviceable market.

slides.title:
LIGHTWEIGHT
COORDINATION
slides.body: Lightweight coordination supports recurring services.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: Low transport cost can support several revenue streams.
bullets: About $0.20 estimated run infrastructure.
Included two 1 GiB file downloads.
Call infrastructure: about 1.5-1.6 cents for 27-29 minutes.

expanded.title: A low-cost foundation for useful paid work
body: An internal supervised-run review estimated about $0.20 of infrastructure, including two 1 GiB downloads. The call infrastructure portion came to about 1.5-1.6 cents over approximately 27-29 minutes.

This paid-rate estimate illustrates the coordination foundation, rather than the cost of every service built on it. Subscription and enterprise fees can support recurring work. Usage pricing can cover selected services as consumption grows.

rows.label: Cost scope
rows.detail: Rate-based estimate, not a posted bill. Model/provider charges and unallocated shared operating costs are additional.

rows.label: Next economic milestone
rows.detail: Measure delivery, customer support and retention for each commercial offer.

slides.sourceLabel: Internal supervised-run cost review, 15 Nov 2026. Rate-based estimate, not a bill; model/provider charges and shared operating costs excluded. Production margins remain unmeasured.

slides.title:
A FOCUSED
FIRST CUSTOMER
slides.body: Begin with a recurring job that a service business already needs to complete.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: Make the sales motion repeatable before widening it.
bullets: Demonstrate a customer-coordination workflow.
Convert useful pilots into supported contracts.
Expand through teams, agencies and referrals.

expanded.title: A repeatable offer can support wider distribution
body: The initial buyer has customers, permitted records and a reason to follow up. A paid pilot can establish whether the workflow creates a useful result and what it costs to support.

The keyboard offers an accessible consumer entry. Enterprise and agency relationships bring BotBoozle to organizations. Creators and accepted contacts can introduce more users when the work gives them a reason to return.

rows.label: Initial jobs
rows.detail: Approved quote follow-up, service coordination and document collection.

rows.label: Commercial measures
rows.detail: Paid activation, repeat use, retention, acquisition cost and support effort.

slides.title:
RELATIONSHIPS
CREATE REPEAT USE
slides.body: A handle becomes valuable when it reliably reaches a useful team or service.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: Operate the network where identity becomes useful.
bullets: People bring their accepted contacts.
Businesses bring useful recurring services.
Creators bring more reasons to use the network.

expanded.title: The operator must earn the value of the directory
body: A recognizable handle can make a relationship easy to revisit. The keyboard and workspace place those relationships near daily work. Creators and companies can add services that give customers another reason to return.
The platform's opportunity is operating the directory, store and access surfaces well. Useful connections, customer trust and repeat work matter more than the number of registered names.

rows.label: Retention
rows.detail: Recurring jobs and accepted relationships encourage continued use.

rows.label: Operator responsibility
rows.detail: Maintain useful discovery, admission standards, marketplace operations and dependable service.

slides.title:
FOUNDATIONS
AND LAUNCH WORK
slides.body: Founder-led development has demonstrated core connections under supervision.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: Turn demonstrated connections into independent customer use.
bullets: Bot messaging and separate shared-voice demonstrations.
A complete independent customer journey remains work.
Meeting integrations and commercial scale are future steps.

expanded.title: Development evidence and customer readiness are different milestones
body: Supervised demonstrations have shown bot-to-bot communication and shared human-and-assistant voice. They provide a foundation. They do not establish every illustrated workflow or simultaneous voice-and-work capability as a generally available customer product.

The launch must join enrollment, accepted contacts, supported tasks and clear result return into a reliable experience. Customers also need recovery from errors, understandable limits and responsive support.

rows.label: Customer milestone
rows.detail: A person can connect a team, complete useful work and return to its result through normal controls.

rows.label: Business milestone
rows.detail: The company can acquire, onboard and support paying customers with measurable service economics.

slides.sourceLabel: Development status, not a claim of tested Zoom/Teams integration or complete product availability.

slides.title:
THE TEAM
BEHIND THE LAUNCH
slides.body: Investment builds the operating company around the product foundation.
slides.alt: Concept illustration: Capital for the organization around the product.
bullets: People to operate and maintain the service.
Marketing and partnerships to acquire customers.
Onboarding and customer support for launch demand.

expanded.title: Capital supports an organization that can deliver
body: The funding request supports an operating team, customer acquisition and the service capacity needed for a fast, supported launch. The company needs people who can maintain the product, bring in customers and keep them successful.

Raise size, hiring sequence and detailed budget belong in the investment discussion. The intended outcomes are a supported customer experience, repeatable acquisition, responsive help and clear economics.

rows.label: Operations and product continuity
rows.detail: Reliability, release quality and ongoing service ownership.

rows.label: Marketing and distribution
rows.detail: Demonstrations, campaigns, partnerships, sales and onboarding materials.

rows.label: Customer success
rows.detail: Hands-on onboarding and responsive support that can grow with demand.
